claims.text: DFT-based SQS simulations can represent atomic-scale chemical disorder in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The SQS models can explicitly incorporate 1 wt.% oxygen impurities in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
Combining SQS with finite-temperature lattice dynamics and electron–phonon coupling calculations will predict electrical conductivity within ±10% of experiment.
The ±10% conductivity accuracy will hold throughout 0–200 K.
The ±10% conductivity accuracy will hold throughout 300–1200 K.
The experimental specimen of bulk HfNbTaTiZr contains 1 wt.% oxygen.
Chemical disorder and oxygen impurities induce local atomic potential fluctuations.
Chemical disorder and oxygen impurities modify the alloy's phonon spectra.
Disorder- and impurity-induced lattice distortions modify electron–phonon scattering rates.
Disorder and oxygen-induced distortions modify the electronic band structure.
Changes in electron–phonon scattering and band structure make the predicted conductivity more representative of real HfNbTaTiZr than predictions from ideal defect-free models.
Existing analytical approaches assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
Perfect-crystal analytical assumptions systematically overestimate or otherwise misrepresent electrical conductivity in disordered, defect-rich samples.
The proposed method is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The claimed validity is limited to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Significantly different oxygen concentrations may fall outside the model's scope.
Finite-temperature phonon dynamics and electron–phonon interactions are uncertain in complex disordered systems.
Validation against intermediate-temperature experimental data mitigates uncertainty in the finite-temperature treatment.
A conductivity discrepancy greater than ±10% at a held-out temperature near 150 K would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Approximately 150 K is proposed both as an intermediate-temperature validation checkpoint and as the held-out falsification benchmark. A datum used for validation or cross-verification cannot simultaneously be genuinely held out.
